abstract: Visual perceptual decisions depend on both how the visual system represents the stimuli and how those representations are read out to guide perception and behavior. Improved visual perception through training, a phenomenon known as Visual Perceptual Learning (VPL), has been partly attributed to adjustments of the readout weights across visual areas to reach better decisions. However, it has been difficult to test whether this reweighting remains at a late stage of the hierarchy or can amplify the readout of whichever hierarchical stage has the most informative representations for the training stimulus. Here, we leveraged DorsalNet, a hierarchical neural network model of the primate dorsal stream, to synthesize motion stimuli that selectively target early or late areas of the primate dorsal pathway. Human observers were trained to discriminate the synthesized stimuli over three days, and transfer was subsequently measured across retinal location and stimulus type. Training improved performance for both stimulus types (early- and late-stage targeting stimuli), but through different mechanisms. Training with late-stage stimuli significantly increased perceptual sensitivity, a gain that transferred across retinal locations. Training with early-stage stimuli produced only a weak, non-significant change in sensitivity; instead, it significantly reduced a conservative response bias, an effect that did not persist at the new retinal location. Specificity indices for stimulus location and type showed different patterns across stimulus categories. A DorsalNet-based model of VPL reproduced both the learning dynamics and these distinct specificity patterns most closely when the model readout was solely plastic for late, rather than early, model layers. Together, these results support a late-stage reweighting account of perceptual learning, in which readout from a preferred, late stage of the dorsal hierarchy is reweighted regardless of the trained stimulus. Under this account, stimuli well matched to the readout stage yield sensitivity gains, whereas poorly matched stimuli afford only weak sensory evidence, prompting observers to compensate by shifting their decision criteria.
